# Agent Transparency: A Review of Current Theory and Evidence

Adella Bhaskara , Michael Skinner, and Shayne Loft

**Abstract—As machines and agents become more autonomous, it has been increasingly clear to human factors/ergonomics researchers and practitioners that agent transparency is a critical issue for effective human–agent teaming. Transparency methods can provide the foundation for establishing shared awareness and shared intent between humans and intelligent machines. However, to date, the existing body of research on agent transparency has not been systematically documented. The purpose of this article is to summarize and evaluate current psychological theories and empirical evidence regarding effective agent transparency in human–autonomy teaming. We start by examining how transparency has been operationalized in the literature by discussing the two prominent theoretical frameworks of human–autonomy teaming. We then present a review of the empirical findings concerning how transparency affects key human–autonomy teaming variables, such as operator accuracy, decision time, situation awareness, perceived usability, and workload. This article includes an overview of the experimental tasks, scenarios, and interfaces that have been used in past studies and synthesizes how transparency has been operationalized and manipulated by prior studies. We then summarize the results and conclude by providing key recommendations for future research.**

**Index Terms—Automation, agent transparency, autonomous systems, human–agent interaction, human–autonomy teaming, unmanned autonomous vehicles.**

## I. INTRODUCTION

HE PREVALENCE and capability of automation and autonomous systems continue to grow and be used in a range of industrial applications in order to reduce human labor and extend work capability and safety [1]. The term “automation” is used to define technology that partially or fully completes a task function that was previously, or conceivably could be, carried out by a human. The degree of automation in a system can vary across a continuum, from the lowest level in which the human takes all responsibility to the highest level in which the system decides everything and acts autonomously [2], [3]. Higher levels of automation imply more responsibility for the automated system, requiring less intervention by the human. High levels of automation are referred to as autonomous systems and are differentiated from the less complex, lower levels of automation that use rule-based systems to achieve specific, predefined outcomes. Intelligent agents embedded in autonomous systems are hardware- or software-based computer systems possessing the following characteristics:

1) autonomy (they are able to operate without human intervention for a significant duration);

2) social ability (they are able to interact and communicate with humans or other agents);

3) observability and reactivity (they are able to perceive the environment through sensors and react to it);

4) proactiveness (they are able to self-direct behavior in anticipation of future events and to achieve mission goals; see [4]).

These autonomous agents have the ability to learn from the environment, have a degree of self-governance and self-directed behavior, and are able to evolve and perform tasks on their own. As a result, they are not directly predictable in their behavior and have a greater capacity to make decisions in uncertain and unplanned circumstances [5]–[7].

Technological innovation and its economic benefits mean that in the future, humans will work more with autonomous agents. For example, in the military aerospace domain, one of the primary goals of using autonomous agents is to minimize the number of operators or to have a single operator supervise multiple unmanned vehicles. The demand for unmanned vehicle systems is rapidly increasing in the defense and security sectors due to their capabilities in surveillance, reconnaissance, and intelligence gathering [8]. Unmanned vehicle capability has also inspired civilian agencies to harness the benefits that these systems provide, and the U.S Federal Aviation Administration predicts the unmanned vehicle industry will be worth \$90 billion by 2025 [9]. As another example, in healthcare, automated decision aids integrate information across disparate data repositories to create treatment recommendations. Separation assurance technology in air traffic control provides recommendations to controllers regarding how to keep aircraft safely separated. Navigation aids in transport vehicles provide recommendations of where and when we should drive.

The intelligence of an autonomous agent, however, is not as flexible or as robust as humans in their capacity to understand patterns of behavior, human intentions, implications, and ethical responsibilities. As task environments in which autonomous agents operate increasingly require higher levels of planning, judgment, and decision making, [10], [11], the role of humans will become more important, particularly in contexts where incorrect decisions have serious economic (e.g., manufacturing) and/or safety (e.g., aviation, medicine, defense) consequences. The involvement of human control in higher level knowledge based behaviors (as opposed to lower level skill based behaviors) is known as human supervisory control [12], or more recently coined “human-on-the-loop.” However, in addition, the supervision of the interactions between human and agent can also be partially achieved by the agent. In this manner, in human–autonomy teaming, the human and the agent collaborate as teammates [13], and they can interact with each other, monitor actions, receive feedback, and provide commands for actions.

The inherent uncertainty in dynamic complex task environments coupled with possible operator complacency and operator skill degradation [2], [14], [15] creates the possibility for operators to make errors by disusing or misusing recommendations made by autonomous agents [16]. Disuse refers to operators disagreeing with and not executing a correct agent recommendation (under reliance), whereas misuse refers to operators agreeing with and executing an incorrect agent recommendation (overreliance). Another issue is that operators can spend significant time trying to verify the accuracy of agent recommendations, and this verification can come at a cost to concurrent task performance [1]. There is an urgent need to develop theories of human–autonomy teaming and to collect a related evidence-base that can be used to communicate to stakeholders the options available for designing autonomous agents that can be most accurately and efficiently used by operators.

One potentially important driver of autonomous agent disuse and misuse is when operators have difficulty understanding the agent or why a certain decision has been made by an agent [15]. Not understanding the accuracy and effectiveness of the agent’s action could in turn decrease operator trust in the system. Implementing automation transparency [17] has been proposed as one method of addressing some of these problematic aspects associated with the interaction between humans and autonomous agents. In a transparent system, information regarding the agent’s actions, decisions, behavior, and intentions is communicated to the operator through an appropriate interface with the aim of improving trust in the system, performance, and operator situation awareness (SA) [18]–[20].

## II. THEORY

Transparency aims to provide operators an awareness of an autonomous agent’s behavior, reliability, and intention. Achieving agent transparency refers to the operator being able to understand why an agent behaves in a particular way [21], to understand an agent’s reliability [20], its tendency for errors [22], and its intended action [23]. Transparency has been further described as a means of sharing intent and awareness between the operator and the agent [24]. Essentially, transparency should facilitate an operator’s comprehension of an agent’s intent, performance, abilities, future plans, and reasoning process [25]. Two key models of transparency have been proposed in the literature: Lyons [24] models of transparency for human–robot interaction and Chen et al.’s [25] SA-based agent transparency (SAT) model.

## A. Lyons’ Models of Transparency

Lyons [24] stated that several factors are important to support effective human–robot<sup>1</sup> interaction. These factors fall under two aspects of transparency: the robot communicating its knowledge of the system and its view of the world (robot-to-human), and the robot communicating its awareness about the state of the human operator (robot-of-human).

1) Robot-to-Human Transparency: In robot-to-human transparency, the information that is crucial to convey to an operator can be described in terms of

1) an intentional model;

2) a task model;

3) an analytical model;

4) an environmental model.

In regards to the intentional model, it is important for the human operator to fully understand the design, purpose, and intent of the robot (and how these match with the operator’s expectations). In other words, the operator needs to understand why and for what purpose the robot (automation) was created, and how the system seeks to perform these actions. For example, if the robot was to override a human directive, the operator should be aware that this could occur and also understand when it could occur and why.

The task model relates to specific actions of the robot. Once the operator understands the design, purpose, and intent of the robot, he or she can begin to analyze the actions of the robot. The robot must communicate to the human its current understanding of the task at hand, its intent in terms of what goals it is trying to accomplish, and its progress in achieving those goals, as well as its capabilities and tendency for errors.

The analytical model is concerned with understanding the underlying analytical structure of the robot decision process (i.e., how the robot is doing the analysis and how it makes decisions). The robot needs to communicate to the human the rationale for its behavior or system recommendations. The awareness that this brings the operator will be useful in uncertain situations, as this enables the operator to take over manual control if necessary. For example, knowing that a robot fuses information from satellite imagery and ground sensors (in order to detect the location of potential emergency zones) would be useful in cases where the ground sensor networks had been compromised.

Finally, the environmental model involves educating the operator about how the system senses information. This involves communicating to the operator about the robot’s understanding of the dynamics of the environment (e.g., for potential hostility and temporal constraints). This will help enhance operator SA during uncertainty and help calibrate the operator’s reliance on the robot.

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280"><sup>1</sup>Lyons [24] used the term robots to refer to systems (agents) that operate under some degree of autonomy.</span></small>

2) Robot-of-Human Transparency: While robot-to-human transparency focuses on the robot communicating to the operator about its knowledge of the work system and its view of the world, robot-of-human transparency focuses on the robot communicating its awareness about factors relating to the human. Lyons [24] robot-of-human transparency is explained through 1) the teamwork model and 2) the human state model. According to the teamwork model, both the human and the robot need to have a shared understanding of each other’s role (i.e., who is responsible for a given task or set of tasks) and of the level of autonomy that the system is operating. Once a shared awareness has been established, according to the human state model, the robot needs to communicate its understanding of the humans cognitive, emotional, and physical state. For instance, the robot needs to sense when the human is distressed or fatigued (e.g., through monitoring the human’s cognitive workload) so that the robot could execute an alert to the human or assume autonomous control if human limitations present a safety concern. In this sense, Lyons’ [24] view of robot-of-human transparency is similar to the concept of adaptive automation (see [26]–[28]).

In summary, Lyons’ models of transparency suggest that for human–robot systems to function effectively, the human needs to understand information about the robot (robot-to-human transparency), and the robot needs to effectively communicate its awareness and understanding of human-centric factors (robotof-human transparency).

## B. SAT Model

Chen et al. [25] proposed a model of transparency called the situation awareness-based agent transparency (SAT) model. The SAT model provides guidance on what information should be communicated to operators to promote agent transparency. The SAT model is inspired by Endsley’s [29] theory of SA; the beliefs, desires, intentions agent framework [30]; and Lee and See’s [16] theory of human trust in automation (purpose, process, and performance).

Endsley’s [29] theory of SA involves the following three levels:

1) perception of elements in the environment;

2) comprehension of those elements;

3) projection of their status in the near future.

The first step in achieving SA is to perceive the status, attributes, and dynamics of relevant elements in the environment. For example, for a military pilot such elements could be perceiving aircraft, mountains, or warning lights (alongside their relevant characteristics, such as color, size, speed, and location). The second step in achieving SA is to comprehend or understand the situation by integrating various elements in light of operator goals. For example, if a military pilot sees three enemy aircraft within certain proximity of one another and in a certain geographical location, he or she must understand that this situation indicates certain things about the aircraft’s objectives. The third step in achieving SA is to be able to project the future state of the task environment. For example, from observing behavior patterns and the location of a threat aircraft, a fighter pilot should be able to project its likelihood of attack. SA is built over time and the projection of future actions (Level 3) is achieved through the knowledge of the status, attributes, and dynamics of the relevant elements (Level 1) and the comprehension of the situation (Level 2). In this manner, SA goes beyond perceiving information about the environment; it involves integrating and comprehending the meaning of that information, comparing it with goals, and projecting future states of the environment. Chen et al. [25] used Endsley’s three levels of SA as the basis for their SAT model. When an autonomous agent is involved in operational contexts, the operator needs to have SA of the agent and its environment—according to Chen et al. [25] this can be attained through agent transparency. The SAT model can be used to identify the transparency requirements necessary to support operator’s SA and increase the probability that they appropriately rely on the agent.

The SAT model also incorporates the beliefs, desires, and intentions agent framework [30], along with the three factors (purpose, process, and performance) that have previously been identified as antecedents for trust development in human– autonomy teaming [16], [31]. Purpose represents motives or intent: It describes the extent to which the autonomous agent is being used according to the designer’s intent. Process represents an understanding of the underlying qualities or characteristics that govern how the system behaves: It describes the extent to which the agent is appropriate for a given task and goals. Performance represents the operator expectation of consistent, stable, and desirable performance or behavior: It refers to the current and historical operation of the agent. On the basis of these three factors, the SAT model proposes that to promote agent transparency the operator should understand:

1) the purpose of the agent or why it was developed;

2) the use and limitations of the agent and whether it is capable of achieving goals in a given task;

3) the reliability, predictability, and capability of the agent.

Following Endsley’s [29] three levels of SA, the SAT model consists of three levels. For SAT Level 1, Chen et al. [25] proposed that the operator should be provided with the autonomous agent’s goals, purpose, and its perception of the status of its environment (What is the agent trying to achieve?). For SAT Level 2, the operator should be provided with information about the agent’s rationale behind its actions or decisions (Why does the agent recommend this action?). For SAT Level 3, the operator should be provided with information regarding the agent’s projection of future outcomes (What does the agent expect to happen if I follow this recommendation?). Chen et al. [25] proposed that incorporating these three SA levels into human–autonomy teaming should improve operator SA of the agent and subsequently increase the accurate use of the agent recommendation as it allows the operator to gain understanding of the agent’s intent, reasoning process, and projected outcomes.

In the following sections, we review the empirical evidence regarding the extent to which transparency can increase the accurate use of autonomous agents by the operator (i.e., proper reliance when the agent is correct, and correct rejection when the agent is incorrect [16]). One additional issue is that operators can potentially be overwhelmed by the increased amount of information presented by transparent agents, which may result in difficulty assimilating information to make supervisory decisions, increasing human decision time, and mental workload. Under some circumstances, these costs to transparency may not be acceptable, even if they do come with more accurate agent use.

## III. EMPIRICAL EVIDENCE

The number of studies that have looked at the effects of agent transparency on key human–autonomy teaming variables has been limited and has not produced consistent results (see Table I). We review the five studies that have manipulated different levels of transparency on the key human–autonomy teaming variables of operator performance, decision time, workload, subjective trust, operator SA, and perceived usability of the interface [32]–[36]. We begin by providing an overview of the experimental tasks, scenarios, and interfaces that have been used in these studies. It is important to do so because the methods of studies have differed markedly, and therefore it is important to keep in mind that many findings may ultimately prove to be context dependent. We then describe how transparency has been investigated, operationalized, and implemented in these studies. We then present the results and draw conclusions from the current empirical evidence regarding the extent to which transparency can facilitate human–autonomy teaming.

## A. Overview of Experimental Tasks

Different experimental tasks, scenarios, and interfaces have been used in the five prior studies. In [32] and [34], participants assumed the role of an operator supervising unmanned vehicles. Participants’ were required to direct these vehicles to carry out missions while managing a commander’s intent and vehicle/environmental constraints. Similarly, in [36],<sup>2</sup> participants guided a convoy of a manned vehicle and an unmanned vehicle through a simulated urban environment—with an agent assisting with the route planning task. Participants were required to reroute the convoy as necessary according to events that occurred. In contrast, in [33], participants’ were required to gather information about an autonomous agent known as the autonomous squad member (ASM), and its status, as they completed a route containing obstacles. In [35], the experimental task involved route planning in a simulated urban environment. Participants had to direct a simulated dismounted soldier team to take an appropriate route as it moved from checkpoint to checkpoint. Participants were to ensure that the soldier team arrived at the destination using the least amount of resources possible.

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280"><sup>2</sup>This study was also reported in [37]–[39].</span></small>

In the majority of these studies, participants were required to make a decision based on the available information provided to them from the environment and the agent. In [32] and [34], participants were given two plan options by the agent. Participants chose to either follow the automated recommendation (Plan A) or choose the alternative plan (Plan B). The reliability of the agent was set at 62.5% [32]. When evaluating plans, participants had to take into account parameters, such as the speed, coverage, and capabilities, of the vehicles. Prior to receiving the mission objective, participants monitored the unmanned vehicle positions and status and received intelligence messages containing either patrol reports, updates on vehicle status, or commander intel messages.

In [36], participants were provided with recommendations for route changes following events and potential route threats. The probability that the recommendation was correct was 66%. Participants could either accept the recommended route or reject it and keep the original route. In addition to route selection, participants in [36] had to 1) respond to SA queries and 2) maintain local security and detect threats or hostile targets. In [35], participants’ task was to direct a soldier team to take an appropriate route as it moved from checkpoint to checkpoint. Participants were given a choice to select from three different routes to ensure that the soldier team arrived at the final destination using the least amount of resources.

Finally, participants in [33] monitored the interface to gain information about the ASM and its status as they completed a route containing obstacles. During an obstacle encounter, the ASM would react by performing an action, and participants’ SA was then measured using situation awareness global assessment technique (SAGAT) [40] queries. While monitoring the interface, participants were also required to detect a target object that appeared in the environment.

## B. Varying Levels of Transparency

Transparency information in prior studies contains plans (or suggestions/explanations) communicated by an agent to the human operator through a computer interface. Transparency increased as the amount of information presented to the operator increased (i.e., transparency information presented at higher levels include transparency information presented at the lower level). However, it is important to note that the type and amount of transparency provided at each level varies across studies. Some but not all studies used the SAT model to discriminate transparency levels (i.e., [32]–[34]), but arguably in many studies the transparency manipulations could be equally well conceptualized by applying Lyons’ [24] models of robot-to-human transparency. Moreover, some studies used different naming conventions to denote different levels of transparency. For the purpose of this review, the more general terms of low, medium, high, and very high transparency will be used (see Table I).

1) Low Transparency: The low transparency serves as a baseline and typically contained basic information, basic plan, and/or the agents’ intent. For example, in [33], at low transparency, participants were provided with basic information, such as status, camera, map, resource indicators, and ASM location. Similarly in [35], participants were shown routes, which were colored to denote relative energy and/or time usage requirements needed to traverse that section of the route. When a choice of two plans was suggested by the agent, participants were shown a basic plan, with no reasoning as to why a particular plan was recommended (e.g., “A1 sector search on friendly boat” [32] and “Change to convoy path recommended” [36]).

2) Medium Transparency: At medium transparency, all five studies added the agent’s reasoning. For example, in [32], factors such as the speed, coverage, capabilities of vehicles, and the environment—which determined vehicle appropriateness and influenced the agent’s recommendation of Plan A over Plan B—were presented in the interface through a text box, as well as through a sprocket (containing different wedge sizes and colors denoting each vehicle appropriateness metric). In [34], participants were shown a “Projected Plan Success” tile, which presented how the agent had weighted each parameter (i.e., time, fuel/endurance, vehicle capability, and sensor coverage) according to its importance. Two statements regarding the agent’s reasoning for Plan A and Plan B were also included (e.g., “Plan A: Hawk is the fastest UAV. Panther has pedestrian avoidance technology. Panther and Hawk are good for searching where visibility may be obscured”). Similarly, in [33], [36], and [35], participants were provided a display that showed:

1) an icon depicting agent’s reasoning;

2) an explanation (e.g., “Change to convoy path recommended. Activity in area: Dense Fog”);

3) text boxes and a bar graph to indicate the reasoning behind the agents’ decisions or suggestions.

3) High Transparency: At high transparency, additional information was presented related to predicted outcomes, pre-dicted consequences, uncertainty information, or additional reasoning of the agent’s decision. At high transparency, in [35], a bar graph was added to the interface to show how specific route choices could impact the resource usage for mission completion. Likewise, in [33], predicted outcomes were shown through an icon; and the magnitude of the predicted resources outcome was indicated by the number of red blocks displayed next to the icon. Similarly, in [34], the projected plan success of each plan (regarding time, fuel/endurance, vehicle capability, and sensor coverage) was displayed through the Projected Plan Success tile; and a projection statement was also added (i.e., “It is expected that Hawk will arrive the quickest, and Panther will move quickly on the base road”).

In [32], at high transparency, participants were told about the projection of uncertainty of the agent’s recommendation. This information was shown through a transparent sprocket wedge, a transparent vehicle icon, and a bulleted statement in a text table (e.g., “It is uncertain how fog will affect speed”). In [36], at high transparency, participants were provided with time of report (e.g., “Change to convoy path recommended. Activity in area: Dense Fog. Time of Report: 1 [h]”). Time of report indicated how current the information was, thus providing added reasoning of the agent’s route recommendation. For example, a report of a shooter that came 6 h ago may not be a current concern, whereas a report of dense fog less than an hour ago may be a serious concern for visibility.

4) Very High Transparency: We classified transparency as very high when further information was added in additional to the information provided in high transparency. Both projected outcomes and uncertainty information were added in [33] and [34] studies. More specifically, participants were presented with basic information (low transparency), reasoning of the agent’s recommendations (medium transparency), projection of future state (high transparency), and additional information regarding the uncertainty of the agent (very high transparency). In [33], the uncertainty of the agent was expressed through semiopaque blocks. For example, one solid red block and one semiopaque red block indicate a certainty of low resource usage with the possibility of moderate resource usage. Uncertainty was also expressed through hazards and field events (displayed using icons surrounded by areas of effect). For example, if the exact location was uncertain, the icon was surrounded by a larger (cf. smaller), semiopaque (cf. opaque) field to indicate that there might be a hazard or event in the general area. In [34], the uncertainty statement contained two points: 1) the agent was uncertain about particular aspects of the task, and 2) the agent was making an assumption to deal with it (e.g., “It is uncertain how long the search will take. The agent assumes that the man will be found quickly”).

## C. Effects of Transparency on Human–Autonomy Teaming

1) Performance: Decision Accuracy and Decision Time: Some studies have measured the accuracy of operators in using automated recommendations, namely hit rates and correct rejection rates [32], [34], [36]. Hit rates refer to the proportion of time participants correctly accept the agent’s recommendation (the inverse of automation disuse, [16]). Correct rejection rates refer to the proportion of time participants correctly reject the agent’s recommendation when it is wrong (the inverse of automation misuse, [16]).

In [32], the medium- and the high-transparency conditions yielded significantly higher hit rates (88%) compared with the low-transparency condition (76%). However, hit rates did not differ between the medium- (87%) and the high-transparency condition (89%). Higher correct rejection rates were also found in the medium- and the high-transparency conditions (74%) compared with the low-transparency condition (55%). Furthermore, participants were significantly more likely to correctly reject the agent’s recommendation when they were presented with the high transparency (81%) compared with medium transparency (67%). These results indicate that while presenting the agent’s reasoning to operators (medium transparency) improved correct rejection rates (cf. low transparency), it was the additional uncertainty information (high transparency) that encouraged the operators to question and correctly reject the agent’s recommendation when it was incorrect (improved correct rejection by an additional 14% compared with the medium transparency). Decision time was defined as the time participants took to make a correct decision (to choose Plan A or Plan B), and decision time did not differ as a function of transparency [32].

Stowers et al. [34] did not include a low-transparency condition. They found highest hit rates in the very high-transparency condition and lowest hit rates in the medium-transparency condition. However, they did not present any accompanying inferential statistics; and therefore it is not clear 1) whether uncertainty information (very high transparency) provided a significant increase to hit rates compared with when projection information was presented without uncertainty information (high transparency), and 2) whether the projection information (high transparency) significantly improved hit rates over and above providing the agent’s reasoning alone (medium transparency). Their decision time data were reported in a subsequent paper [41] and was found to be significantly longer in the very high-transparency condition than in the medium-transparency condition.

Wright et al. [36] measured operators’ accuracy in accepting and rejecting agent recommendations in Experiments 1 and 2. In Experiment 1, hit rates did not differ between the three transparency conditions. However, participants in the mediumtransparency condition were significantly more likely to correctly reject the recommendation (81%) compared with participants in the low- and the high-transparency conditions (51%). No difference was found in correct rejection rates between the low- (46%) and the high-transparency (56%) conditions. The overall time taken to make decisions did not differ between the three transparency conditions. Participants’ performance on a secondary task involving target detection also did not differ between the transparency levels.

In [36], Experiment 2, hit rates, and correct rejection rates did not differ between the low-, medium-, and high-transparency conditions. No differences in decision time were found either. Participants’ secondary target-detection task performance was marginally higher in the medium-transparency condition compared with the high-transparency condition. In Experiment 1, participants in the medium condition had significantly higher correct rejection rates compared with the other two conditions. These results were not replicated in Experiment 2. The only difference between Experiments 1 and 2 was the amount of information presented. In Experiment 2, at low transparency, participants were provided with more information via map icons. At medium transparency, the agent’s reasoning included how each piece of information was factored into the agent’s recommendation: “Recommend revise convoy route: Potential IED (H[igh]), Potential Sniper (M[edium]), Dense Fog (L[ow]).” At high transparency, participants were provided with the time of report for each piece of information received by the agent: “Recommend revise convoy route: Potential IED (H), TOR: 1 [hr]; Potential Sniper (M), TOR: 2; Dense Fog (L), TOR: 4.” That is, in Experiment 2, more information was presented at each transparency level, and additional reasoning was added for the medium- and high-transparency conditions. Taken together, results from these two experiments suggest that although pre-senting an agent’s reasoning can have a positive effect on operator performance, adding further information could diminish this advantage.

Wright et al. [35] investigated the effect of transparency on concurrent task performance (as measured by the total resources used in a route planning task). In Experiments 1 and 2, the route planning task involved participants directing a simulated dismounted soldier team to take an appropriate route; and participants had to ensure that the team arrived at the destination using the least amount of resources. Wright et al. [35] found that the resource usage (in both Experiments 1 and 2) did not differ between the three transparency conditions. In Experiment 2, a robotic asset was added to the soldier team and participants had to ensure that the team arrived at the final destination with sufficient resources of battery and fuel. Participants presented with low transparency preserved less fuel than those in either the medium-transparency or the high-transparency condition. Additionally, fuel preservation was lower in the high compared with the medium-transparency condition, suggesting that the addition of predictive information in high transparency may have actually hindered operator performance. For battery usage, no significant differences were found. They also measured the time participants spent at each checkpoint (as they guided a soldier team through their chosen route). Only in Experiment 2 did Wright et al. [35] find that as transparency level increased, the time spent at each checkpoint also increased. Specifically, the time spent at each checkpoint in both the medium-transparency and the high-transparency condition was longer compared with the low-transparency condition (when only basic information was presented), and no difference was found between the medium-transparency condition (when agent’s reasoning was added) and the high-transparency condition (when predictive information was also present).

2) Workload: Workload has been measured both subjectively and objectively. Subjective workload has been measured using the National Air and Space Administration Task Load Index [42] in three of the studies, and no differences have been reported in subjective workload as a function of transparency [32], [33], [36]. Workload has also been measured objectively by eye tracking in two studies. In [36], cognitive workload was evaluated using ocular indices of pupil diameter, fixation duration, and fixation count. In Experiment 1, there were no effect on these ocular indices as a function of transparency; in Experiment 2, pupil diameter was larger in the low-transparency condition compared with both the medium- and the high-transparency conditions indicating higher workload. Mercado et al. [18]<sup>3</sup> did not find an effect of transparency on either fixation duration or pupil diameter.

3) Situation Awareness: Out of the five prior studies, only two have examined the impact of transparency on SA. Selkowitz et al.’s [33] required participants to use the interface to gain information about the ASM and simulated squad’s status as they completed a route containing obstacles. During an obstacle encounter, the simulation paused and participants’ SA were assessed using SAGAT—relating to the ASM status (Level 1 SA), reasoning (Level 2 SA), and projected outcomes of its action and reasoning (Level 3 SA). SAGAT query Level 1 SA did not differ across the four transparency conditions (low, medium, high, and very high). However, high transparency had the highest Level 2 SA score and was significantly higher than the medium-transparency condition. For Level 3 SA, the high-transparency condition had the highest score and was significantly higher than either the low-transparency condition or the medium-transparency condition. These results suggest that the predicted outcome information (high transparency) improved operator Level 2 SA and Level 3 SA more so than when the uncertainty information was added (very high transparency), supporting the notion that providing too much information to operators is not necessarily going to be advantageous (see [43]).

In Wright et al. [36], while performing the route selection task and the target-detection task, at each mission participants were required to respond to SA queries via real-time probes. These SA probes enquired participants about:

1) objects and persons in the environment (Level 1 SA);

2) reasoning behind the participants’ choices (Level 2 SA);

3) projecting future status of their convoy based on their understanding of upcoming threats along their route (Level 3 SA).

In Experiment 1, high transparency had the highest Level 1 SA and was significantly higher than the medium transparency, which had the lowest. The differences between the three transparency conditions (low transparency, medium transparency, and high transparency) were not significant for Level 2 SA or Level 3 SA. In Experiment 2, no differences in SA were found between conditions.

4) Trust in Automation: The effect of transparency on operator subjective trust was investigated in [32], [33], and [36]. In [32], subjective trust was measured using a modified Jian Trust Survey [44] that assessed participants’ trust of the system on two stages of human information processing: 1) the display of information (trust during “information analysis”), and 2) trust during decision and action selection [2]. The results from the information analysis subscale showed no differences between the three transparency conditions. Mercado et al. [32] expected these results because although the reliability of the agent’s recommendation was not perfect, the information supporting agent transparency was 100% accurate. However, the results from the decision and action selection subscale showed higher trust when high transparency was presented compared with low transparency. These results suggest that operator trust in the agent’s recommendation increased as the system became more transparent (i.e., when agent’s reasoning and uncertainty was provided).

Selkowitz et al. [33] also used the modified Trust in Automated Systems questionnaire [44] to measure history-based trust. History-based trust was defined as the ongoing, changing relationship of trust that is influenced by the operator’s interaction with the agent. The average history-based trust score was higher when participants were provided high transparency compared with low or medium transparency; however, trust of the very high-transparency automation did not differ from the other conditions. Thus, presenting an agent’s reasoning and the projected state of the system (high transparency) increased trust, but not when uncertainty information was added (very high transparency). In [36, Experiment 1], subjective trust was lowest in the medium-transparency condition and was lower compared with the high-transparency condition. In [36, Experiment 2], trust scores did not differ between the three transparency conditions.

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280"><sup>3</sup>This was the same study as Mercado et al. [32]; however, results from the eye-tracking measures were only available in [18].</span></small>

5) Perceived Usability: Three studies have investigated the effect of transparency on operator perceived usability of the interface (i.e., [32], [34], [36]). The System Usability Scale [45] was used in [32] and [34] to measure users’ feelings of usability (efficiency, efficacy, and satisfaction) with the interface (e.g., “I think that I would like to use this system frequently”). Mercado et al. [32] found no difference in usability ratings between medium transparency (when agent’s reasoning was present) and high transparency (when agent’s uncertainty was added), although usability scores under these conditions were higher compared with the low transparency. Stowers et al. [34] found that while high transparency (when projected plan success was added) resulted in the highest perceived usability, the very high-transparency condition (when uncertainty was further added) had the lowest perceived usability. Nonetheless, they did not report inferential statistics. Wright et al.’s [36] reported that in Experiment 1 when an agent’s reasoning was present, the perceived usability was lower than when either only the basic plan was given or when the level of transparency information was greatest (when basic plan, agent’s reasoning, and further reasoning were added). However, perceived usability in Experiment 2 did not differ as a function of transparency.

6) Summary of Results: This section contained a review of prior studies that have examined the effects of transparency on operator performance (accurate use of agent’s recommendations), decision time, SA, trust, perceived usability, and workload. In some studies, operators actually performed better when agent’s reasoning was given without the addition of higher levels of transparency [35], [36]. The exception to this was in [32] where correct rejection rates increased when uncertainty information was also presented along with agent’s reasoning (compared with when only agent’s reasoning was presented). However, in [36, Experiment 1], providing extra reasoning to operators did not make a difference to performance (correct rejection rates did not differ from baseline where no reasoning was provided). These results highlight the importance of information quality over quantity—that operator performance can be affected by the type of information they receive, but extra information can sometimes be unnecessary.

With regards to decision time, the results have been mixed. While some studies found that increased transparency does not affect decision time [32], [36], other studies found that decision time increased with increased transparency [34], [35, Experiment 2]. However, there has been no strong evidence to suggest that transparency increased operator workload.

For operator SA, the addition of predicted outcomes improved operator Level 2 SA and Level 3 SA more than when both pre-dicted outcomes and uncertainty information were present [33]. However, when increased reasoning was added in the higher transparency levels, no differences were observed, except only in [36, Experiment 1] where the high transparency improved operator Level 1 SA compared with the medium transparency.

For operator trust, the evidence suggests that—up to a point— operator trust increases as transparency increases. However, there have been inconsistencies in the type of information pre-sented for high transparency (e.g., uncertainty versus predicted outcomes); hence, it is not clear which aspect of the high transparency is responsible for improving trust. In [32], providing information about agent’s reasoning did not impact operator trust (when compared with when only basic information was provided), however operator trust increased when agent’s reasoning was also presented with uncertainty information. In contrast, in [34], the availability of predicted outcomes significantly improved trust over and above agent’s reasoning alone; however, when uncertainty information was added to predicted outcomes, participants’ trust in the system waned slightly, resulting in no significant differences with the other transparency conditions.

The results regarding perceived usability have not been consistent. While in [36, Experiment 1], the presence of agent’s reasoning decreased perceived usability compared with when this information was not present, increased agent’s reasoning actually improved perceived usability. Additionally, while pre-senting agent’s reasoning and agent’s uncertainty was perceived to be useful in [32], one study [34] found that the additional uncertainty information had the lowest perceived usability. These inconsistent findings might be due to differences in the interfaces used across studies and the way the different levels of transparency were presented.

In summary, the empirical evidence suggests that transparency does seem to affect operator performance, SA, perceived usability, and trust. However, it is still unclear how much and what type of transparency information should be provided— as some of these studies suggest that while higher levels of transparency may improve some of these measures, the highest transparency level did not always produce the best outcomes.

## IV. SUMMARY AND DIRECTIONS FOR FUTURE RESEARCH

Two models of transparency for human–autonomy teaming have been proposed: Lyons’ [24] models for human–robot interaction and Chen et al.’s [25] SAT model. The studies reviewed here have mainly used the SAT model to operationalize transparency levels, and there is emerging evidence to suggest that transparency can increase the accurate use of autonomous agents by human operators. However, evidence regarding which precise level of transparency yields the most accurate use of agents has been far from consistent. The fundamental assumption underlying prior research is that providing increasingly transparent information to the human operator (regarding the agent’s intent, performance, future plans, and reasoning process) should allow the operator to develop an accurate mental model of the agent and its behavior—leading to calibrated trust in (and more appropriate reliance on) the system and ultimately leading to a more accurate use of the agent. In contrast, some findings actually suggest that appropriate care should be taken when presenting transparency information to avoid overwhelming the operator.

In our opinion, there are two main reasons for the lack of consistent results across studies. First, the requirements to achieve system transparency are likely to be highly context dependent. An important goal for future research is to attempt to replicate effects across different task domains in a more programmatic series of studies. The scientific value of replication in establishing the reliability of effects has received much recent attention in the psychological literature [46], [47] and is particularly vital when the resulting knowledge will potentially be used by practitioners and stakeholders in safety-critical settings [48].

Second, although the SAT model has been used as the primary overarching framework to operationalize transparency in human–autonomy teaming, there is no strong available evidence regarding the underlying psychological mechanisms that are impacted by increased transparency. We argue that one of the key ways to move forward is to discover how increased transparency can change how human operators process task information. Discovering the psychological mechanisms by which transparency can influence the use of autonomous agents will significantly advance our ability to assess, predict, and explain the impact of agent transparency and play a key role in guiding future approaches to designing and evaluating autonomous agents. For example, with the exceptions of [33] and [36], prior studies have not directly tested whether agent transparency increases operator SA.

One hypothesis is that increased transparency—if appropriately designed—should minimize or otherwise change the information the operator is required to process to verify agent recommendations (as possibly measured by eye-tracking technology). If increased transparency can increase the ease of cross checking the validity of recommendations by highlighting key information, then transparency should mitigate the impact of two key factors known to reduce the extent to which operators seek to validate recommendations: 1) high concurrent task demands and 2) high perceived automation reliability [49], [50]. Chen et al. [25] argue that the three SAT levels may not be absolutely necessary to achieve transparency. For example, in a time-sensitive situation, an operator may only need to know the agent’s proposed action (Level 1) and the projected outcome (Level 3) to make a decision. However, this has not been tested. Additionally, future research needs to investigate whether time pressure or additional workload would compromise the impact of transparency.

To date, the transparency literature has focused primarily on the SAT model and what Lyons [24] refers to as robot-to-human transparency. Lyons’ [24] robot-of-human transparency emphasizes the importance for the robot to effectively communicate its awareness and understanding about factors relating to human. While the teamwork model component of Lyons’ robot-of-human transparency has been discussed in the literature [51], [52], the human state model component of the robot-of-human transparency is a concept that needs to be further explored. If the agent can be trained to detect operator cognitive state (e.g., via heart rate variability, skin conductance) or the current attentional focus of the operator (e.g., via real-time eye-movement data), it could cue the operator’s attention to the transparent information when it is most likely necessary, increasing the probability that human operator will comprehend the significance of information that potentially contradicts the agent’s advice, thereby improving human–autonomy teaming.

Finally, it will be important for future research to include studies with expert participants in higher fidelity simulations, where possible. This is crucial to ensure that the research is appropriately translated back to industry because it will provide a stronger test of the extent that outcomes from more basic research can be applied to operational settings. In addition, the high-fidelity simulations with experts will develop understanding of how experts and novices differ (or not) in how they strategically deal with autonomous agents.

With the development of more complex systems, researchers have started to investigate factors—such as agent transparency— that could improve human trust and reliance on autonomous agents. An empirically supported model would be of great utility in guiding the design of an interface that supports transparency and in testing the varying effect of different forms of transparency on human–autonomy team performance. The two models of transparency for human–autonomy teaming proposed by Chen et al. [25] and Lyons [24] provide a great starting point; however, future research needs to tease apart exactly what type of transparency information would be beneficial for the operator and in what contexts. Finally, future research needs to also investigate the underlying processes that explain why transparency information facilitated operator performance (e.g., by providing direct evidence that operator mental model and SA improved as a result of agent transparency). Understanding the underlying psychological processes is fundamental to designing an interface that supports transparency in human–autonomy teaming.
